title: 城市河流修复
instructions: Reading Passage 1 has ten questions. You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–10, which are based on the passage below.
passage:
Restoring Urban Rivers

For most of the twentieth century, many planners treated a river running through a city as a problem to be solved. Waterways were straightened into concrete channels, or buried in pipes beneath roads, so that floods could be moved quickly out of the city and land beside the water could be used for housing or industry. By the 1990s, however, engineers in several European and North American cities had begun to question this approach. Rivers were living systems, they argued, and could cool overheated streets, shelter wildlife and provide public space. The movement to bring these waterways back to the surface became known as urban river restoration.

The best-known type of project is daylighting, in which a buried stream is uncovered and returned to the open air. Supporters often describe daylighting as a simple case of undoing past mistakes, yet the actual work is rarely straightforward. A restored river must be designed to carry storm water that arrives in sudden, heavy bursts, which is different from the steady flow of a natural country stream. Engineers therefore combine natural features, such as stones, curves and planted banks, with hidden engineering, including wider culverts and overflow basins. Critics sometimes claim that these hybrid designs are too artificial to count as true restoration, but many ecologists reply that any river within a city is shaped by people and that the aim is a system that works, not a perfect copy of nature.

Evidence of success is mixed. In one fictional three-year study used here as an illustration, a city uncovered a short stretch of river beside a former car park. Water temperature dropped, and records from local residents showed that more birds visited the area in summer than before the project. However, the number of fish in the new channel did not rise as expected, a result the study team linked partly to the distance between the site and the nearest healthy river source.

Cost is the main reason projects are delayed. Removing a concrete channel and reshaping a bank can be far more expensive than carrying out basic repairs to the existing channel, and local councils frequently face pressure to spend money on schools or transport instead. In response, some cities have divided large schemes into stages, completing small sections whenever funding becomes available. This approach spreads the cost over many years, though it can leave a restored stretch looking isolated until surrounding pieces are finished.

Public support is another factor that shapes outcomes. When residents are involved in decisions about planting or the design of footpaths, they tend to take greater care of the finished area. Where projects have been introduced without any consultation, by contrast, some users have complained that safe routes to work were lost when paths were narrowed to make space for vegetation.

It would be easy to read the growth in the number of daylighting schemes as proof that the approach has been settled. It has not. Debates continue over how much engineering is acceptable, how success should be measured, and who should pay. Real restoration, in the sense of a river returning to the state it had before the city was built, is almost never achieved. The realistic goal, most practitioners now agree, is a river that is healthier and more useful than the one it replaces, while being honest about the compromises this involves.

title: 种子库的科学价值
instructions: Reading Passage 2 has ten questions. You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 11–20, which are based on the passage below.
passage:
The Scientific Value of Seed Banks

A seed bank is a collection of seeds stored under controlled conditions so that they remain able to grow long after they were collected. The largest international facilities hold hundreds of thousands of samples, each representing a particular kind of plant gathered from a specific place. The main reason for keeping such collections is insurance. Farming depends on a remarkably small number of crop types, and a disease or a change in climate can threaten a popular variety very quickly. A stored sample may contain genes that allow a related plant to survive heat, salt or pests, and these genes can be crossed into crops that people rely on.

Storage is less simple than it sounds. Seeds must be dried to a low moisture level and then kept cold, which slows the chemical processes that eventually stop them from growing. Even so, seeds do not last forever. Many remain capable of growth for decades, but some, such as those of certain tropical trees, lose their ability to sprout within a short time however carefully they are handled. For these troublesome species, researchers depend on living plants in gardens or on very cold storage, which is far more costly.

A second value of seed banks lies in what they can tell scientists about change over time. Because seeds were gathered at known dates and locations, comparing old samples with newly collected ones can reveal shifts in the size, shape or genetics of a species. In one fictional study used here for practice, researchers grew seeds collected from a meadow on the same site in three different decades. The plants from the oldest seeds flowered later than the recent ones, which the authors treated as a possible sign of adaptation to warmer springs, though they themselves suggested that other explanations could not be ruled out.

Such use raises practical difficulties. A seed sample is only useful if it has been properly recorded: where it came from, when it was gathered and how it was stored. Where records are incomplete, results can be misleading, because a difference between two samples may reflect the way they were kept rather than any real change in the plants. Some collections from the mid-twentieth century were stored with limited detail about the conditions involved, and researchers must therefore be cautious when using them.

Finally, seed banks are not only scientific tools; they are also the subjects of political discussion. Countries disagree about who owns the genetic material of plants that grow within their borders, and about whether stored samples should be freely shared. International agreements have tried to balance these interests, but the rules remain complex, and some researchers argue that they slow down the work of comparing collections across countries. What is clear is that the collections are more valuable when they are shared, yet sharing is exactly what disagreements make difficult.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
questions.prompt: According to the first paragraph, why could a stored seed sample be important to farmers?
choices: It may supply genes that help crops resist difficult conditions.
It can be planted instead of any crop that fails.
It allows farmers to grow a wider range of plants for profit.
It holds seeds that are larger than modern varieties.
answers: It may supply genes that help crops resist difficult conditions.
questions.explanation: 原文 'A stored sample may contain genes that allow a related plant to survive heat, salt or pests, and these genes can be crossed into crops'，热、盐、害虫即 'difficult conditions'，可用于改良作物。B、C、D在文中均无依据。

the genetics of tropical trees and meadow grasses
the growth of seeds kept in warm and cold conditions
plants grown from seeds taken from several different meadows

questions.explanation: 原文 'researchers grew seeds collected from a meadow on the same site in three different decades'，'same site' 对应 'the same place'，'three different decades' 对应 'different years'。B、C、D均无依据。
questions.evidence: In one fictional study used here for practice, researchers grew seeds collected from a meadow on the same site in three different decades.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
questions.prompt: Why might comparisons of old and new samples give wrong conclusions?
choices: Old seeds are usually too small to measure accurately.
Differences may come from storage conditions rather than the plants themselves.
Newly collected seeds are rarely recorded properly.
Living plants in gardens grow faster than stored seeds.
answers: Differences may come from storage conditions rather than the plants themselves.
questions.explanation: 原文 'a difference between two samples may reflect the way they were kept rather than any real change in the plants'，'the way they were kept' 即储藏方式，'rather than any real change' 对应 'wrong conclusions'（假差异）。A、C、D在文中无据。
questions.evidence: Where records are incomplete, results can be misleading, because a difference between two samples may reflect the way they were kept rather than any real change in the plants.

questions.instruction: Complete each sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.
questions.prompt: Seeds are first dried so that their _____ level is low, and then they are stored in the cold.
questions.explanation: 原文 'Seeds must be dried to a low moisture level and then kept cold'，题干 'their _____ level' 对应 'a low moisture level'，故填 'moisture'。
questions.evidence: Seeds must be dried to a low moisture level and then kept cold, which slows the chemical processes that eventually stop them from growing.

questions.instruction: Complete each sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.
questions.prompt: For species that are hard to store, researchers depend on living plants or on very cold storage, which costs much _____.
questions.explanation: 原文 'very cold storage, which is far more costly' 与题干 'costs much _____' 同义，'far more costly' = 'costs much more'，只填 'more'。
questions.evidence: For these troublesome species, researchers depend on living plants in gardens or on very cold storage, which is far more costly.

questions.instruction: Complete each sentence with NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.
questions.prompt: Collections are more valuable when they are shared, but disagreements make _____ difficult.
questions.explanation: 原文 'the collections are more valuable when they are shared, yet sharing is exactly what disagreements make difficult'，空处为 'sharing'。
questions.evidence: What is clear is that the collections are more valuable when they are shared, yet sharing is exactly what disagreements make difficult.

title: 图书馆入会咨询
instructions: Questions 21–30. You will hear a conversation between a woman and a library assistant about joining the library. Listen and answer the questions.
script:
Woman: Good morning. I'd like to join the library, please. Could you tell me what I need to do?
Assistant: Of course. But before we start, could I take a few details? So, your name …
Woman: It's Marta Nowak.
Assistant: Thank you. And the address?
Woman: Fourteen Bell Street, Flat Three.
Assistant: Our records still show Fourteen Bell Street. Is that your current address?
Woman: That's right, I've moved. It's Twelve Bell Street now.
Assistant: I'll correct that. Twelve Bell Street it is. Could you confirm the postcode?
Woman: It's E nine, zero A B.
Assistant: E nine, zero A B. Thank you. Now, membership costs eleven pounds fifty a year for adults. Oh, wait, I'm looking at the student rate. For an adult it's twenty-four pounds ninety-five.
Woman: Twenty-four ninety-five, fine.
Assistant: And your membership will start on the third of March.
Woman: I was told it could start next week, on the twenty-fourth of February?
Assistant: Sorry, no. You only need to wait for the new card, which is issued on the third of March. Before that, a guest card lets you borrow books, but not at the weekend. The library opens at nine on weekdays, though … and nine thirty on Saturdays.
Woman: I see. How many items can I take out?
Assistant: Ten books at a time, and we have a family rate as well. What interests you most?
Woman: Mainly local history. And I'd like to use the computers.
Assistant: You're in luck. We run a free talk for new members on the second Thursday of every month, at six forty-five, in the reading room. As for the computers, the website lists all of them, so I'm sure you'll find that useful.
Woman: Great. What do I need to bring?
Assistant: Just one form of photo identification. It used to be two, but we've changed the rule. Is there anything else?
Woman: I don't think so. Thank you very much.

speech:
Good morning. I'd like to join the library, please. Could you tell me what I need to do?
Of course. But before we start, could I take a few details? So, your name …
It's Marta Nowak.
Thank you. And the address?
Fourteen Bell Street, Flat Three.
Our records still show Fourteen Bell Street. Is that your current address?
That's right, I've moved. It's Twelve Bell Street now.
I'll correct that. Twelve Bell Street it is. Could you confirm the postcode?
It's E nine, zero A B.
E nine, zero A B. Thank you. Now, membership costs eleven pounds fifty a year for adults. Oh, wait, I'm looking at the student rate. For an adult it's twenty-four pounds ninety-five.
Twenty-four ninety-five, fine.
And your membership will start on the third of March.
I was told it could start next week, on the twenty-fourth of February?
Sorry, no. You only need to wait for the new card, which is issued on the third of March. Before that, a guest card lets you borrow books, but not at the weekend. The library opens at nine on weekdays, though … and nine thirty on Saturdays.
I see. How many items can I take out?
Ten books at a time, and we have a family rate as well. What interests you most?
Mainly local history. And I'd like to use the computers.
You're in luck. We run a free talk for new members on the second Thursday of every month, at six forty-five, in the reading room. As for the computers, the website lists all of them, so I'm sure you'll find that useful.
Great. What do I need to bring?
Just one form of photo identification. It used to be two, but we've changed the rule. Is there anything else?
I don't think so. Thank you very much.

title: 野外考察行前说明
instructions: Questions 31–40. You will hear a teacher giving a talk to students about an upcoming field trip. Listen and answer the questions.
script:
Teacher: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for coming. This is the briefing for next month's field trip to the coastal wetland. A few details have changed since my last email, so please listen carefully. We're going to the north hide instead of the east hide, because the east hide is still closed for repairs. We will now meet at half past seven in the main car park, not half past eight. That's been changed because the bus company needs the vehicle back earlier, and the journey takes an hour and a half.

The cost of the trip has also changed. The first letter said eleven pounds seventy, but after checking the coach price again, the final cost is twelve pounds forty per student. You should pay by Friday the fourteenth of March, not the twenty-first as the email said. If you have already paid the old amount, the school office will sort it out with you.

Now, what you need to bring. A packed lunch, and you will need waterproof boots, as the paths may be muddy. Gloves are no longer required; we've decided it's warm enough at this time of year. If you have any questions about the trip, call the science department on double oh seven, five five nine, one three four eight. Please don't call the school reception, as they don't have the details.

The wetland centre has asked us to follow some rules. You can walk along the boardwalk without a guide, but please stay on it, as the mud around it is unsafe. We will record our bird counts with the centre's own sheets, and they will forward the results to the website later.

Finally, our return time. It was going to be four forty in the afternoon, but I've now been told the bus will leave the centre at four fifteen instead. Thank you, and I'll see you all at the meeting point.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

choices: Students must be led along it by a guide.
Students can use it freely but must keep to it.

choices: The bus will leave the centre at 4.15.

questions.evidence: It was going to be four forty in the afternoon, but I've now been told the bus will leave the centre at four fifteen instead.
